title: Blessed are you poor (Luke 6:20–26)
hook: Luke's beatitudes are blunt, with woes to the rich

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the lake of Genesareth, a boat full of fish, and Peter asking Jesus to depart. Your line was fear not.

Matthew sets the beatitudes on a mountain: blessed are the poor in spirit. Luke tells a different scene. Jesus has spent the night praying on a mountain, picked his twelve, and come down. He stands, Luke says, in a plain place, a level stretch of ground, with a great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon. Sick people push to touch him. He lifts his eyes to his disciples and speaks, and what he says is shorter than Matthew's version, and sharper.
screen: `A NIGHT OF PRAYER, THEN DOWN.` → `A PLAIN PLACE, A GREAT CROWD.` → `SHORTER, AND SHARPER.`

segments.voice: Luke's first beatitude, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." Not poor in spirit. Poor. And not they. You. Jesus is looking at real people in front of him and talking straight to them. Luke has four blessings: you poor, you who hunger now, you who weep now, you who are hated for his sake. Then he turns the coin over with four woes. The first: "But woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation." Woe to you that are filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you that now laugh. Woe when all men speak well of you. Each blessing has its matching woe. Some readers hear woe not as a curse but as a cry of grief: alas for you. On that reading, Jesus isn't wishing harm on the comfortable; he's warning that comfort can be the whole reward, and then it's spent. So which is it, poor or poor in spirit? Catholics read both Gospels as true and hold them together. Matthew names the heart that knows it needs God. Luke won't let that become only an inner feeling: real hunger and real poverty are what God sees first. The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for the poor, and says that love is inspired by the Gospel of the beatitudes. Some saints took Luke literally. Francis of Assisi handed even his clothes back to his father, in front of the bishop, and walked away with nothing.
screen: `NOT POOR IN SPIRIT. POOR.` · `FOUR BLESSINGS, FOUR WOES.` · `WOE AS A CRY: ALAS FOR YOU.` · `A PREFERENTIAL LOVE FOR THE POOR.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE YE POOR.`

segments.voice: Think of who you're likely to pass today: someone outside a store, a coworker who's struggling, a family on a parish list. Pick one, decide what you could give, money, food, time, a real conversation, and picture looking them in the eye, the way Jesus looked at the crowd on the plain, as people he called blessed. If you pray, hold that person before God by name.
Blessed are you poor. Luke's first beatitude, spoken face to face on a level plain, paired with a woe for the rich. Today's word.
Your line: blessed are you poor. Not they, but you, face to face. That's day four hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's sermon on the plain at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and parishes run food pantries, Saint Vincent de Paul conferences and collections for the poor as a regular part of parish life.

original.note: Greek: the poor, the word used for beggars. Luke's word for the people Jesus calls blessed.

trapdoor: what you thought: blessed are the poor is a nice saying about humility.
what it means: in Luke, Jesus looks at people who are actually poor and hungry and says you are blessed, then warns the rich.
what a scholar hears: ptochos is the Greek word for the destitute beggar, not just someone of modest means.

chat.says: Matthew says poor in spirit. Luke just says poor. Which one is right?
options: Catholics hold both: Matthew names the heart that needs God; Luke, the real poor.
Matthew is right; Luke's version is a copying mistake that dropped a word.
Neither; Jesus meant only people who had taken vows of poverty.
chat.meaning: Catholics read both Gospels as true together: poor in spirit is the heart that knows its need, and Luke insists real poverty is what God sees first.
